claims.text: Conventional Cr–Mo steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as tempering temperature is varied.
Controlled impurity or solute content influences the ductile–brittle–ductile transition in Cr–Mo steel.
Cr–Mo steel undergoes a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow intermediate tempering-temperature window.
Impurity or solute segregation at grain boundaries causes the intermediate-temperature loss of ductility.
The proposed initial material is homogenized, as-quenched or normalized Cr–Mo steel with minimal initial impurity segregation.
The proposed intervention is a series of progressively higher-temperature tempering treatments with controlled impurity or solute levels.
The intermediate tempering regime is expected to induce significant impurity segregation.
Phosphorus and tin can segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed Cr–Mo steel system.
Enhanced diffusion at intermediate tempering temperatures promotes impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation weakens grain-boundary cohesion.
Weakened grain-boundary cohesion causes temper embrittlement.
At lower tempering temperatures, segregation is insufficient to cause the proposed loss of ductility.
At higher tempering temperatures, impurity redistribution or dissolution restores ductility.
Maximum segregation coincides with the sharpest drop in ductility.
Ductility recovers when tempering occurs outside the critical temperature window.
Cr–Mo steel tempered outside the critical range has relatively high ductility because grain-boundary impurity segregation is minimal.
The transition is sensitive to the precise tempering temperature and impurity or solute levels.
Changes in tempering temperature or impurity content can suppress the transition.
The exact transition window and magnitude of ductility loss depend on impurity identity, impurity concentration, and minor compositional variations.
